wu2015.title: Multi-events earthquake early warning algorithm using a Bayesian approach
wu2015.author: S. Wu, M. Yamada, K. Tamaribuchi and J. L. Beck
wu2015.venue: Geophysical Journal International, Volume 200, Issue 2, pages 791-808
wu2015.quote: However, during the 2 months after the main shock on March 11, because of the significantly increased seismicity around the region, 44 inappropriate warnings (missed and false alarms) were issued among the 70 early warnings broadcast to the public.
quotes: During the 2011 M9 Tohoku earthquake in Japan, an earthquake early warning (EEW) system operated by the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) provided the first early warning 5.4 s after the first P-wave detection, which was before the S-wave arrival throughout all areas in Japan.
Over 70 per cent of the inappropriate warnings were caused by multiple concurrent events (referred as the 'multi-events' problem in this paper).

During the period of active seismicity after the Tohoku earthquake, the JMA EEW system sometimes treated the data from multiple events as a single earthquake. As a result, some of the near source stations of the second event were treated as far source stations of the first event. This led to a significant overestimate of magnitude and caused false alarms.

kodera2021.title: Developments of the Nationwide Earthquake Early Warning System in Japan After the 2011 Mw 9.0 Tohoku-Oki Earthquake
kodera2021.author: Yuki Kodera, Naoki Hayashimoto, Koji Tamaribuchi, Keishi Noguchi, Ken Moriwaki, Ryo Takahashi, Masahiko Morimoto, Kuninori Okamoto and Mitsuyuki Hoshiba
kodera2021.venue: Frontiers in Earth Science, Volume 9, Article 726045
kodera2021.quote: The overprediction was caused by M4.5 and M4.0 earthquakes in January 2018 that occurred simultaneously, ~400 km away from each other (JMA, 2019a). The magnitude of the M4.5 earthquake was overestimated because the system calculated the magnitude with displacement amplitudes of the M4.0 earthquake.
quotes: From October 2007 to March 2010, the system successfully provided accurate ground motion predictions, and the prediction score was as high as ~80%. However, the prediction score decreased to 28% in Japanese fiscal year 2010 (from April 2010 to March 2011) due to the occurrence of the Tohoku-Oki earthquake (JMA, 2014).

IPF (Tamaribuchi et al., 2014) is a PSM algorithm that has been employed in the JMA EEW system since December 14, 2016 (JMA, 2016) to reduce the risk of overprediction due to the misassociation of P-wave picks for multiple simultaneous earthquakes.

PLUM (Kodera et al., 2018) is a wavefield-based algorithm (Hoshiba, 2013; Hoshiba and Aoki, 2015) that has been implemented since March 22, 2018 (JMA, 2018) to provide accurate ground motions for large earthquakes with nonnegligible finite faults and for intense earthquake sequences for which PSM algorithms could fail to estimate correct source parameters.

For the association of P-wave picking data, IPF also takes into account velocity amplitudes in addition to travel time differences, to discriminate the occurrence of multiple simultaneous earthquakes from a single large event.
125 and 25 OBSs of S-net were introduced in the system on June 27, 2019 and on March 24, 2020, respectively
the system overpredicted ground motions for multiple simultaneous earthquakes, failing to associate P-wave travel times and mislocating the hypocenters
kodera2021.note: Open access. PDF downloaded from frontiersin.org and read as text on 2026-08-22; the tilde characters above are the paper's approximately-equal glyph. The 28% figure is for Japanese fiscal year 2010, which runs April 2010 to March 2011 and therefore ends three weeks after the main shock - it is not a figure for the aftershock period alone.
supports: prediction score ~80% before, 28% for Japanese fiscal year 2010

hoshiba2011.title: Outline of the 2011 off the Pacific coast of Tohoku Earthquake (Mw 9.0) - Earthquake Early Warning and observed seismic intensity
hoshiba2011.author: Mitsuyuki Hoshiba, Kazuhiro Iwakiri, Naoki Hayashimoto, Toshihiro Shimoyama, Kazuyuki Hirano, Yasuyuki Yamada, Yuzo Ishigaki and Haruyuki Kikuta
hoshiba2011.venue: Earth, Planets and Space, Volume 63, Issue 7, pages 547-551
hoshiba2011.quote: By the fourth 'forecast', 8.6 s after the first trigger, the magnitude was estimated to be 7.2 and seismic intensity was expected to be 5-lower for central Miyagi prefecture (around Sendai city) and the fourth 'forecast' was a 'warning' to the general public in the Tohoku district.
quotes: The JMA EEW system was triggered for the Mw 9.0 earthquake when station OURI detected the initial P wave at 14:46:40.2, Japan Standard Time, March 11 (JMA, 2011a, b). The first EEW 'forecast', the first of 15 announcements, was issued 5.4 s later.
The EEW 'forecast' is issued to advanced users when events are estimated to be M 3.5 or larger, or when the expected seismic intensity is 3 or greater.

The JMA EEW system issued one 'warning' to the general public in the Tohoku district before the start of strong ground motion. It was earlier than the S wave arrival and 15 s earlier than strong ground motion (intensity 5-lower or greater) at the closest station to the epicenter.
hoshiba2011.note: Received 12 April 2011, revised 21 May 2011, accepted 22 May 2011, online published 27 September 2011, per the PDF front matter. The publisher PDF at link.springer.com redirects to an authentication endpoint; read on 2026-08-22 from the Internet Archive capture of the original TERRAPUB PDF, http://web.archive.org/web/2018id_/http://www.terrapub.co.jp/journals/EPS/pdf/2011/6307/63070547.pdf. Curly quotation marks in the source are transcribed here as single quotes. This source is why the prose says 'the first early warning' and not 'the first public warning': the announcement 5.4 s after the first P-wave detection was an EEW 'forecast', which JMA issues to advanced users. The warning to the general public was the fourth forecast, 8.6 s after the first trigger.
supports: the first EEW announcement for the main shock, 5.4 s after station OURI detected the initial P wave at 14:46:40.2 JST on 11 March 2011, was a 'forecast', not the public warning
JMA EEW is graded 'forecast' (advanced users) and 'warning' (general public)

The number of aftershocks in the sequence, and how many of the 70 public warnings were misses as opposed to false alarms - Wu et al. give the combined count only.
The exact end date of the 'two months after the main shock' window that yields 44 of 70; the paper says only 'the 2 months after the main shock on March 11'.

The claim, reported on the OUP page's abstract, of 'over 90 per cent reduction in the number of incorrect warnings' for the proposed Bayesian method - a retrospective simulation figure, not a production one, and not re-read against the PDF.

Whether the 5.4 s figure Wu et al. give as 'the first early warning' is the same announcement Hoshiba et al. call the first EEW 'forecast' is inferred from the two papers agreeing on the number and the event; Wu et al. do not use JMA's forecast/warning grading.
